images.caption: A stage that keeps the fort alive all day long with live performances of bhangra, gatka, gidda, comedy, games, dholi etc. Several prizes are here to be won each day.

images.caption: A glorious history from the past depicted through the means of technology, to entice, enlighten, educate, enthrall and inspire. images.filename: Plan of the Gobindgarh Fort near the formidable wall (38939184591).jpg
images.caption: As we pass the formidable walls of the Gobindgarh Fort and the nearly vertical steps leading onto it, we also notice a large billboard showing the plan/ map of the fort. After being closed to the public for several years, as it had been under the control of the Indian army until very recently (see notes earlier in this album), a bit of restoration and tourist oriented features have been added. So apart from being a plan of the fort premises, this signboard also points out the location of various facilities like the toilet, food court etc. (Amritsar, Punjab, northern India, Nov. 2017)

images.filename: No, not wine, the mannequin is seen carrying a keg of gunpowder (25064587038).jpg
images.caption:
It was some 20min to closing time and we still had to check out the Toshakhana (gunpowder magazine), and is possible, go find dinner in one of the food outlets on the premises of the Gobindgarh Fort.

Getting to the Toskakhana was easier said than done. The path to the facility is straightforward enough, but all lights had been switched off due to the ongoing Spirit of Punjab performance. And not expecting any more visitors that late, the Toshakhana caretakers had switched off the lights in the building as well. So getting there meant a lot of touch, smell and feel, helped in little with the on-board flashlight of our cell phones, which we took turns in using so as to not run out of juice completely on any one phone. In the entrance hall of the Toshakhana is this mannequin of a Sikh gentleman carrying a keg on his shoulder. No, that is not wine, that's a (gun)powder keg. (Amritsar, Punjab, northern India, Nov. 2017)

images.filename: I didn't quite get the idea behind blocking the steps with a shield and spears (38050089135).jpg
images.caption:
The two ladies sitting at the foot of the steps fortunately moved off pretty quickly, and so I was able to take this shot of the almost vertical set of steps leading up the walls and to the bastion of the Gobindgarh Fort in Amritsar. My sis in law loved this view. I like it how they have created a barrier using a touch of history (a shield and two cross spears) rather than a thick chain with a notice 'Visitors not permitted beyond this point'-

that would have ruined the view completely. Bravo Amritsar! (Amritsar, Punjab, northern India, Nov. 2017)

images.filename: A long shot of the formidable wall inside the Gobindgarh Fort (38936482981).jpg
images.caption:
We are now in the Gobindgarh Fort grounds at last, past three gates.
We are greeted by a set of steep stairs, rising almost vertically onto the walls of the fort. The steps have been closed to the public by means of a shield and cross spears. Photography of that would be severely hampered by the two ladies sitting at the steps, or so I thought.

They fortunately moved off a few moments later- they had been waiting for their menfolk who were a bit behind. (Amritsar, Punjab, northern India, Nov. 2017)

images.filename: Watercolour of Gobindgarh Fort, by Charlotte Canning, 7 February 1860.jpg
images.caption:
Watercolour of Gobindgarh Fort, Amritsar, by Charlotte Canning, 7 February 1860.
‘Govindgarh. The Fort at Umritsur, 7 Feb. 1860’  Gobindgarh Fort Amritsar.⁣
Many of her watercolours were published in a book titled 'Sketches From A Howdah: Charlotte, Lady Canning’s Tours: 1858-1861' (2018) by F. S. Aijazuddin.
